extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, literary scholars, and students of narratology
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Genette's five-category narratological taxonomy to analyze how a story is told across order, duration, frequency, mood, and voice; use the categories to identify techniques (e.g., flashback, scene, focalization) and judge their effect and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: ORDER (Anachrony)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation between the chronological order of story events and the order of their narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes types and sub-dimensions: Analepsis — flashback; narration of an event after later events have been told; Prolepsis — flashforward; narration of an event before its chronological place; Achrony — events without identifiable temporal location. Also consider Reach — how far back/forward the anachrony extends, and Extent — how long the anachrony lasts. When analyzing or judging, identify whether narration follows or rearranges chronological sequence and the narrative effects achieved by those rearrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: DURATION
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation between story-time and discourse-time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify stretches of narrative by how discourse-time maps to story-time: Ellipsis — story-time elapses with no discourse-time (gap); Summary — discourse-time shorter than story-time; Scene — discourse-time roughly equal to story-time (often dialogue); Stretch — discourse-time longer than story-time (slow motion); Descriptive Pause — discourse-time elapses with no story-time. Use these distinctions to assess pacing choices and their effects on emphasis, rhythm, and reader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: FREQUENCY
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation between how often an event occurs and how often it is narrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify frequency patterns: Singulative — narrating once what happened once; Multiple-Singulative — narrating n times what happened n times; Repetitive — narrating multiple times what happened once; Iterative — narrating once what happened multiple times. Evaluate how repetition or singularity of narration shapes meaning, emphasis, or thematic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: MOOD (Distance and Focalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the narrative is presented; regulates information flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two sub-axes: Distance (modes of speech presentation) — Narrated speech (fully transposed), Transposed speech (indirect discourse), Reported speech (direct discourse/quoted). Focalization (perspective) — Zero focalization: omniscient narrator who knows more than any character; Internal focalization: narrator knows what one character knows (can be fixed, variable, or multiple); External focalization: narrator knows less than the character and reports only external phenomena. Use mood to analyze how much information is given, from what epistemic standpoint, and how speech is rendered, affecting sympathy, suspense, and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: VOICE
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider three sub-axes: Time of Narration — Subsequent (past-tense narration after events), Prior (predictive/prophetic), Simultaneous (present-tense), Interpolated (between actions, e.g., epistolary, journals). Narrative Level — Extradiegetic (narrator outside the story-world), Intradiegetic (narrator inside the story-world), Metadiegetic (narrator inside an embedded story). Person — Heterodiegetic (narrator absent from the story they tell), Homodiegetic (narrator present as a character), Autodiegetic (narrator is the protagonist). Analyze voice to determine narrator position, temporal relation to events, and implications for authority, reliability, and intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative use of the five axes
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework's application for critique and craft decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any narrative can be exhaustively analyzed across these five axes — order, duration, frequency, mood, and voice — and craft choices judged for their coherence, effect, and necessity. Use the axes jointly to assess whether narrative techniques cohere, support intended effects (e.g., suspense, irony, characterization), or should be revised for clarity, emphasis, or reader engagement.
